name: Daria Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the afternoon shift on a bottle-filling line that packs cooking oil. I set the fill heads, watch the weight checks and stop the conveyor when a capper starts leaving loose lids. My two-year technical diploma helps when a sensor fails, but most good decisions start with listening to the line. I share a flat with my partner; our income is sound, I earn above the usual operator rate, and I have more than six months of expenses saved. Several plants nearby hire operators, though I would rather keep this team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that a little software help with batch paperwork is welcome. The fill weight and lid seal still need an operator to check them against real bottles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My line hours and higher rate look safe in this mild picture, and the savings can absorb a quiet week. I only worry that a copied batch number could pass through a neat form unnoticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the filler and check the first and last bottles of each batch by hand. In the first year I would continue using AI now and then to draft a shift note, while checking every number against the line log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A shorter report might get me home sooner, but a loose lid still sends me back to the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which number is easiest to copy wrongly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The batch code when we switch from one oil size to another. If that code is wrong, tracing a bad seal becomes much harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after a quiet week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That our savings cover it and I am still on the shift rota. I would not cut our ordinary spending over a small office shortcut.

say: **Batch paperwork** may get quicker while operators still check fill weight and lids.
The **line log** remains the source for batch codes.
think: My **higher rate** and savings protect us from a short quiet week.
A copied **batch code** can hide inside a polished form.
do: **Keep** running the filler and testing bottles by hand.
**Use** occasional AI drafting for shift notes while checking numbers against the log.
S0.quote: A shorter report might get me home sooner, but a loose lid still sends me back to the machine.
fieldNote: Her **current AI use** is occasional note drafting, not automated quality control.
Strong **savings** and nearby plants keep a minor change from threatening household income.

steps.text: Keep running filler and checking bottles against the line log

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the planners and buyers will feel this before the filling line. If software changes our production order, I want the shift lead and quality checker to see the new batch sequence before we start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster office might send more changeovers into one shift, which could stretch the team but does not automatically cut my pay. I could learn a proven scheduling tool if another line has used it without mixing batches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare one AI-built batch plan with our last month of changeovers. If the plant offers an actual funded class on paid time, I would take it in the first year and practise entering a changeover while the quality checker watches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a wrong sequence, not frightened for my job yet. A mislabeled oil pallet can undo a whole fast afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare in the two plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cleaning time between oil types, the label roll and the batch code for each pallet. I would circle any plan that squeezes out a required cleaning step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the other line has not proved the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using the signed paper schedule and ask for a supervised trial before any live batch runs from the new plan. A slide presentation would not be proof.

say: **AI planning** reaches buying and sequencing before hands-on filling.
The **quality checker** should see each changed batch plan before production.
think: More **changeovers** could strain the shift without certain wage loss.
I would trust a **new planner** only after a real line proves it.
do: **Compare** an AI batch plan with a month of changeover records.
**Take** a funded paid-time scheduling class if an actual place opens.
feel: **Uneasy** about a mistaken batch sequence, while pay appears secure.
S1.quote: A mislabeled oil pallet can undo a whole fast afternoon.
fieldNote: Her **steady approach** requires a proven line plan and a quality checker beside any practice.
She distinguishes **office automation** from the operators still setting and cleaning the filler.

steps.text: Take funded AI scheduling class only with paid place and quality checker supervising practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI could handle the plans and buying by 2028, while capable robots that can set up and inspect a filling line arrive around 2031. We need a route into maintaining those machines before the operator roster shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the higher shift-lead rate if a robot handles changeovers and checks without my team. Six-plus months saved and several nearby plants give me room, but neither guarantees the same wage in a machine-heavy plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance manager for a funded controls course with an actual place and paid hours, including safe isolation of the filler. If the place opens I would complete it; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local maintenance role only if qualified and its hours and pay cover our flat and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the machine date is close enough to affect my next job choice. I would rather learn why the capper stopped than wait to be the last person checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe isolation training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Locking the filler out before a hand reaches the capper, testing that power is off and recording who restores it. A robot fault light is not permission to open a guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no funded place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid shift and check posted maintenance vacancies at nearby plants for their entry requirements. I would not spend the household cushion on an unrecognised course.

say: **2028 AGI** changes plans before capable line robots around 2031.
Operators need a route into **safe machine maintenance** before rosters shrink.
think: A robot could remove my **shift-lead premium**.
Savings and nearby **plants** do not guarantee equal maintenance pay after my line rate disappears.
do: **Request** funded paid-time controls training with safe isolation practice.
**Complete** training if an actual place opens.
**Apply** for posted local maintenance work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about losing the higher line rate.
S2.quote: A robot fault light is not permission to open a guard.
fieldNote: Her **income risk** comes from capable setup and inspection robots around 2031, not 2028 paperwork.
Her **training and application** need a real funded place, safe isolation, qualification and a bill-covering local posting.

steps.text: Complete funded filler-controls course with safe isolation if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local maintenance role if qualified and pay/hours cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant five years is enough to run real changeover trials before capable robots arrive around 2034. I want operators who know the capper involved in writing the lockout steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could qualify for maintenance while the line still needs me, but only if the course teaches actual controls and safe isolation. I would not leave a good wage for a maintenance title without a posted opening at workable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading shifts and ask for a supervised robot-changeover trial on paid time. If the plant offers a funded controls course with a real paid-time place, I would finish it; in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted local maintenance post only if qualified and the wage and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the 2034 line roster, but the longer lead lets me check what the machine really does. I would rather have five years of paid robot-controls practice than five years of rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should supervise a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A maintenance technician and the quality checker, with an operator able to stop the line. We would record wrong caps, missed cleaning and any guard opened unexpectedly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as workable pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough regular hours and base wage to pay our flat, food and travel without drawing from savings each month. A flashy overtime figure would not be enough.

say: **2031 AGI** gives time for real changeover trials before robots around 2034.
Operators should help write **lockout steps** for robot work.
think: A proper **controls course** could move me into maintenance.
A new **job title** is useless without a posted opening at bill-covering pay.
do: **Finish** funded controls training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local maintenance work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about the 2034 line roster, with time for paid practice.
S3.quote: I would rather have five years of paid robot-controls practice than five years of rumours.
fieldNote: Her **trial request** remains a request until the plant offers paid time and supervision.
The **maintenance move** depends on safe practical training, an actual course place and adequate local wages.

steps.text: Finish funded controls course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local maintenance post if qualified and pay/hours cover bills
Request paid supervised robot-changeover trial with technician quality checker and operator stop control

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell new operators a decade lets them learn the machine from the inside before a robot takes over setup. AGI may change the production plan in 2036, with capable hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be older but still expect to earn for many years after 2039. The savings help with a changeover between jobs, not with quitting work, and I do not want my technical diploma to sit unused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the filler shift and put one fifth of each paid shift premium into savings starting now. If the plant funds a paid-time controls course with an actual place, I would complete it before 2039; in the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted local maintenance job only if qualified and its base pay and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Measured, with plenty of time to build another skill. A ten-year AGI warning is useful only if the controls training hours appear on a real rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save from the premium?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The premium varies, so one fifth of each paid amount is manageable. That would add new money to our reserve without pretending the existing savings are extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plant still needs skilled setup and pays the present rate, I would stay while gaining controls training. I would move only for a real local offer with safe duties and workable pay.

say: **2036 AGI** changes plans before capable line robots around 2039.
Young operators can learn **machine internals** during the long runway.
think: I expect to need **wages** long after 2039.
Existing **savings** cushion a move but cannot replace a career.
do: **Keep** leading the filler shift and save one fifth of paid premiums.
**Complete** funded controls training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local maintenance work if qualified and base pay covers bills.
feel: **Measured**, with time to build a second skill.
S4.quote: A ten-year AGI warning is useful only if the controls training hours appear on a real rota.
fieldNote: Her **long working horizon** makes a switch into maintenance credible, not retirement.
New **premium savings** come from paid earnings; course and job moves retain funding, paid-time and local pay conditions.

steps.text: Keep leading filler shift while it pays the present rate
Save one fifth of each paid shift premium
Complete funded controls course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local maintenance job if qualified, safe, with bill-covering base pay and hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time before robots can set up the filler as well as my shift. An actual funded controls place on paid time, safe isolation practice and a posted local maintenance job at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I can teach a new operator where a capper jams. I want to understand who fixes the robot when its guard stays closed.

portrait: **Daria Garcia**, 27, leads a cooking-oil bottling line and has a two-year technical diploma.
She lives with her **partner**, earns above the usual operator rate, has more than six months saved and many nearby plants.
She uses **AI occasionally** for shift notes and checks batch numbers against the real line log.
She is **anxious** in the fast scenario because capable robots could remove her shift-lead premium around 2031.
She seeks **funded controls training** and posted local maintenance work with safe isolation duties and bill-covering pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time before capable robots could remove her line setup and shift-lead premium.
whatWouldHelp: An actual **funded course place** on paid time and a posted local maintenance role at adequate pay would help.
Practical **safe isolation** training would prepare her to work around machine guards.
headlineQuote: I can teach a new operator where a capper jams. I want to understand who fixes the robot when its guard stays closed.
